item.title: GALLERY WALK! BOUND BY NATURE — Fri Oct 2, 5:00 PM — Juniper Art Gallery
item.description:
Bound by Nature
20 Original Ornamental Insect Illustrations
by Jonathan Nash
Opening Reception:
First Friday Gallery Walk, Oct 2, 5-8:00pm
Special music by Elias Fisher, 6-7:30pm
Bound by Nature is a commissioned series of twenty original Art Nouveau-inspired illustrations created for the wedding of Erica Nadolkski and Jordan Evans.
Each poster celebrates a different insect personally selected by the bride, pairing it with native flora and elements of its natural habitat. Drawing inspiration from vintage natural history plates and the decorative compositions of the Art Nouveau movement, every illustration is framed by ornamental motifs unique to its featured species, incorporating elements from its life cycle, host plants, and surrounding ecosystem.

item.title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature — Sat Oct 3 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Sat Oct 3 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Sat Oct 3 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers

item.title: One Person, No Vote: A Lecture and Q&A with Carol Anderson — Tue Oct 6, 7:00 PM — Buskirk-Chumley Theater
item.description: One Person, No Vote: How Voter Suppression is Destroying Our Democracy, a lecture and Q&A with Carol Anderson Carol Anderson is the Robert W. Woodruff Professor of African American Studies at Emory University. She is the author of several bestselling books including: The Second: Race and Guns in a Fatally Unequal America (2020); One Person, No Vote: How Voter Suppression Is Destroying Our Democracy (2018), which was long-listed for the National Book Award in Non-Fiction; and the critically-acclaimed White Rage: The Unspoken Truth of our Racial Divide (2016), which won the 2016 National Book Critics Circle Award for Criticism and was also a New York Times Bestseller, a New York Times Editor’s Pick, and listed on the Zora List of 100 Best Books by Black Woman Authors since 1850. Professor Anderson is also the author of Eyes Off the Prize: The United Nations and the African-American Struggle for Human Rights, 1944-1955 (Cambridge University Press), which was awarded both the Gustavus Myer

item.description: Conflict in Contemporary Asante: The Trickster Chief A chieftaincy dispute began in the small town of Juaso between the chief and the queenmother but extended its reach for several decades to involve the community, a Paramount Chief, the Asantehene, the government, and many others. The junior chief performed tricks that publicly challenged authority – paralleling the tricks of Ananse, the Ghanaian trickster. Throughout, the dispute rested on the longstanding Asante principles of kinship and of law (both following and challenging them). It invoked the play of power and politics in the range of forces that integrate chieftaincy and modernity in Ghana.About the Speaker Beverly J. Stoeltje is Professor Emerita of Anthropology and Folklore and Ethnomusicology at Indiana University Bloomington. item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. item.description: CLACS Faculty Research Symposium welcomes Luis A. González, Librarian for Latin American, Spanish & Portuguese, Latino, and European Studies, and an Adjunct faculty in History at Indiana University as he presents: Books in Formerly Sacred Spaces: The Story of a Public Library, a President, and an Artist — Jiquilpan, Mexico, 1941 Abstract: This presentation considers the Gabino Ortiz Public Library, notably founded by President Lázaro Cárdenas in his hometown of Jiquilpan, Michoacán, in 1941. As part of his national cultural project, President Cárdenas opened the library within a repurposed church which also houses murals by José Clemente Orozco depicting events from the Mexican Revolution. This case study presents a compelling opportunity to examine the intersections of state cultural policy, collective memory, and the social imaginary of the library in modern Mexico. item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery.
